title: Solar panels in winter: do they still earn their keep?
description: Short days, low sun, the odd blanket of snow — winter is unkind to solar panels, but not in the way most people assume. Cold panels are efficient panels; it is the missing daylight, not the temperature, that costs you.

body.heading: Cold helps, darkness costs
paragraphs: A solar panel converts sunlight into electricity, and its electronics actually work slightly better in the cold — panels lose efficiency as they heat up, which is why a bright, frosty spring day can out-produce a hazy hot one. Winter's real tax is geometry: fewer daylight hours, and a sun that stays low, striking the panels at a slant and through more atmosphere.

Expect a clear seasonal rhythm rather than failure: a system that covers a household's usage across the year typically banks its surplus in summer — through export payments or net metering where available — and draws on that credit through the darker months. Judge a system on its twelve-month total, never on a December week.

body.heading: Snow, and the two cheap wins
paragraphs: Snow is a smaller villain than it looks. Panels are smooth, dark and tilted, so a covering layer often slides or melts off faster than snow on the roof around them — and a thin dusting still lets some light through. Never climb up to sweep them; the lost day's generation is worth far less than a ladder accident.

The cheap winter wins are elsewhere: run big appliances in the bright middle of the day when your panels are producing, and keep an eye on your generation app for sudden drops, which usually mean shading or a fault rather than weather. Winter does not break solar economics — it just pays its share of the bill in a different season.

takeaway: Winter cuts solar generation through short, low-sun days — not cold, which actually helps panels — so judge a system on its full-year total, not a dark week.
